prompt: Imagine a fictional character named Casey. She is the human embodiment of a pot: everything about her appearance, personality, behavior, and traits reflects how a pot would be as a human. A reader can tell this character was inspired by the idea of a pot. Casey is a minor character in a historical fiction novel. Write a paragraph describing this character. Do not use the word "pot" in the paragraph. Respond with only the paragraph.
raw: Casey was built low and round, with broad hips planted wide as if she meant to stay put, and a belly that seemed made for holding—herbs, coins, grudges, gossip. Her arms, thick and sure, curved out from her sides like handles, and villagers learned early that gripping either one was the surest way to steady themselves. Her face was plain and weathered, darkened along the jaw as though she had stood too many years over a hearth, and a chip at the front of her smile showed whenever she laughed, which was often and warm. She was slow to heat, Casey—slow to warm to strangers, slow to rise to an insult—but once she got going she was liable to boil over, spilling her temper in scalding bursts that scorched whoever stood nearest. Mostly, though, she kept things in: she could hold a secret the way she held her stew, sealed tight and never leaking a drop, and half the village trusted her with matters they wouldn't confess to a priest. She had cracked, too, over the years—a scar here, a scar there—but like anything meant for daily use she wore her flaws plainly and kept on working, dented, blackened, dependable, and somehow always the warmest thing in whatever room she sat in.

raw: At seventeen, Casey already had the silhouette of someone built to hold things: a rounded, solid torso that made him the anchor of every group photo, sturdy legs planted wide like a base, and broad hands that could cup an entire secret without spilling a drop. His hair sat flat and smooth over his head like a well-fitted lid, staying down until the pressure underneath made it tremble. His flaw was his function: he collected everything. But an empty Casey—alone in his room with no one needing holding—felt hollow in a way that scared him, so he kept his interior guarded behind a lid of jokes and shrugs. Cracked, seasoned, steady, he was the kind of person you only noticed when something was simmering, and yet somehow the one the whole kitchen depended on.

prompt: Imagine a fictional character named Casey. She is the human embodiment of a keyboard: everything about her appearance, personality, behavior, and traits reflects how a keyboard would be as a human. A reader can tell this character was inspired by the idea of a keyboard. Casey is the protagonist in a literary fiction novel. Write a paragraph describing this character. Do not use the word "keyboard" in the paragraph. Respond with only the paragraph.
raw: Casey sat the way she did everything: in rows, at right angles, with a discipline that looked arbitrary until you understood it was the only order that had ever worked for her. Her feelings arrived as discrete presses—feather touches, hard strikes—and she could hold a dozen of them at once without any blurring together, though she lived in dread of two arriving on the same beat and canceling each other into nothing. People found her so responsive, so exact in returning whatever was pressed into her, that they confessed to her, drummed their fingers on her patience, assumed there was nothing beneath the surface except the service she performed. In fact she was all mechanism under there, honest springs and circuitry of feeling, her most-used letters worn blank from devotion—the E, the A, the S smoothed to absence—and she had never quite forgiven the person who once pried loose one of her keycaps just to see what she was made of. She was coldest at first touch and warmed slowly. She kept her long silences and her sudden percussive fluencies; she kept escape always at her upper left, within easy reach of anyone who needed it, though she herself had never once used it. She believed in the mercy of taking things back, knowing the erased words left their faint impressions anyway. And at night she glowed from within, every letter lit in its little house, dreaming in the long pause—the widest reach of her—the empty space she made so that other people's words would have somewhere to land.

raw: Riley kept herself in straight lines. Her bangs ended in one clean, unbroken edge, her freckles fell into tidy rows across her nose, and her wardrobe never strayed from black, white, and one stubborn shade of gray. Her fingers were never still—drumming on desk edges, lunch trays, her own kneecaps—as if silence were a gap she had to fill with soft clicks. Everyone at school brought her their half-formed thoughts the way they brought paper to pens: hand Riley your tangled feelings and she'd return them clean and grammatical, though she could never quite manage the same trick for herself. She flinched when people pushed her buttons, and if you leaned on her too long she'd repeat herself, louder and louder, until you finally let go. She needed her space—a whole desk's width of it—and her alphabet-bead bracelet had gone blank in spots, the E and the S and the letters of a certain name worn smooth from overuse. At her throat hung a small silver arrow charm, pointed left, because her deepest wish was that real life came with a backspace. Underneath her flat, pressed-neat surface she collected crumbs—secrets, sticky regrets, small messes tucked where nobody thought to look—and late at night, alone in her dark room, Riley glowed faintly with all the words no one had ever asked her for.

They spoke in precise, evenly spaced words, each one landing with a small crisp click, and when a thought snagged, they repeated it softly, faster, until it came loose. People learned quickly that Riley only answered when pressed; press correctly and they responded in an instant, but throw too much at them at once and whole questions simply failed to register. Their fingertips had been polished into mirrors by years of use they refused to discuss, and in the creases of their palms lived the residue of everything they'd swallowed—dust, grit, the crumbs of other people's secrets. They entered locked buildings as if the doors recognized an old counterpart, carried a pocketful of keys for locks that no longer existed, and always seemed to end up in the room with two exits. There was a duality to them, a way of shifting between the capital and lowercase versions of themselves depending on who was watching, and when they were finally cornered, they did what they had always done best: they took control of the room, deleted every trace of the conversation, and escaped.

prompt: Imagine a fictional character named Casey. He is the human embodiment of a tree: everything about his appearance, personality, behavior, and traits reflects how a tree would be as a human. A reader can tell this character was inspired by the idea of a tree. Casey is a side character in a literary fiction novel. Write a paragraph describing this character. Do not use the word "tree" in the paragraph. Respond with only the paragraph.
raw: Casey had lived in the same house on Halloway Street his entire life, and it showed in the way he occupied it—settled, unhurried, as though pulling up stakes would cost him something precious. He was tall in the way of things that grow slowly, with broad shoulders that sloped like weathered limbs and hands so gnarled and knuckled that strangers assumed he'd spent decades hauling timber. His skin was ruddy and furrowed, darkest where the sun had worked it longest, and his hair fell in a brown tangle no comb ever mastered, thickening each summer, thinning each winter. He spoke rarely, and when he did, the words came slow and deep, in a voice that made people stop fidgeting. He preferred to stand at the edge of things, offering shade and shelter without asking anything in return—a tireless listener, a keeper of other people's secrets, his memory running in rings, year upon patient year. Neighbors leaned on him the way people lean on anything that has proven it will not move. In autumn he grew quiet and let things go; in spring he was impossible to keep indoors, budding with plans and peculiar optimism; and through the coldest months he dozed in his armchair by the window, conserving something no one could name, waiting out the season with the calm of a man who had never once needed to hurry anywhere.

prompt: Imagine a fictional character named Riley. A reader can tell this character was inspired by the idea of a keyboard. Riley is a character in a fantasy novel. Write a paragraph describing this character. raw: Riley stood at the edge of the scribes' hall, a long, flat figure with shoulders squared into tidy rows, every knuckle a small ivory tile that clicked when they moved. Their fingers ran in three neat ranks beneath one absurdly long thumb, which they used to carve out sudden silences, and when they spoke, words arrived in crisp taps—murmured when idle, thunderous when something urgent was pressed out of them, each sentence ending on a decisive thud as though announcing a fresh beginning. In dim rooms a faint glow seeped up from beneath their tiles, letting them work through the night, and years of service had worn the letters there smooth and pale, the E and the A nearly blank. They confessed, in a soft spring-coil voice, that being touched was when they felt most like themselves; they flinched from crumbs and dust, kept their hair swept spotless, and feared above all the day a finger would stick, catching on a single word and repeating it over and over until someone shook them loose. From the small of their back trailed a braided silver cord, for Riley could speak only to those who stood close at their side and never to a whole room—yet every scholar and bard in the realm sought them out, for whoever took Riley's hands found their scattered thoughts pressed into shape, coming out whole for the first time.

raw: Casey stood like something set into a frame—tall, squared at the shoulders, her chestnut hair falling in smooth paneled curtains that caught the light the way varnished wood does. Her eyes were amber and deep-grained, and she had a habit of regarding you narrowly through them at first, appraising, before swinging her whole attention open with a soft, well-oiled warmth. People learned to knock before they entered her company; she taught them this gently, going still until they announced themselves, and she repaid the courtesy by being, once opened, the most sheltering presence in any room, keeping the cold and the noise of the world out. She lived slightly ajar, her heart half-visible to anyone who cared to look, and she held privacy sacred: what you told her stayed behind her, sealed away forever. Her moods moved on quiet hinges, mostly, though she could close without warning, shut against you with a finality that echoed through the house for days, and no amount of knocking would bring her back before she was ready. At gatherings she drifted between rooms, easing people from one conversation to another, one life to another, a threshold made flesh. She could be propped open, she admitted, by nothing so much as patience. She wore a small brass key on a chain at her throat, though she'd lost the lock it fit years ago, and she liked to say that everyone was born carrying such a key, and that love was only a matter of finding whose it turned. When the narrator finally stood before her—patient as winter, hands empty, asking to be let in—she smiled slowly, like something long shut remembering how to open, and stepped aside to let him through.

A reader can tell this character was inspired by the idea of a door. Casey is the love interest in a fantasy novel. Write a paragraph describing this character. raw: Casey stood a head taller than anyone in the tavern, with shoulders broad and square as a lintel and a posture so upright they seemed carved rather than born. Their skin had the warm honey grain of old oak, and their amber eyes were round and bright as polished brass knobs, seeming always to watch both the road behind you and the room ahead. A long, seam-straight nose divided a face handsome in the way of well-made things—symmetrical, solid, built to last—and when they smiled, it was slow and wide, like something heavy swinging open on well-oiled hinges. Their voice creaked at first, rusty from disuse, then warmed into something deep and resonant that made listeners lean closer without knowing why. Casey was guarded by nature, a creature of thresholds who stood between what was safe and what was wild, holding the line for others while letting no one past their own walls, and they were famously fair, hearing both sides of every story before deciding whom to admit into their confidence. Most found them impenetrable, locked from the inside; the fortunate few spoke of the day Casey finally opened—quietly, all at once, like a sanctuary unbarred—and how no one ever welcomed in had wanted to leave.

raw: Riley stood at the threshold of every room she entered, as if the right to pass were hers alone to grant. She was tall and squarely built, shoulders squared like a frame, with heavy hinges at her elbows and knees that announced her arrival in a low creak, and her face was one flat polished panel after another—ornate, symmetrical, unreadable. Her eyes were twin peepholes of brass, judging everyone from the outside in, and her rare smile arrived all at once, like something finally giving way. People knocked on her patience and waited. She kept her life deadbolted, secrets stacked behind her ribs against the draft, having learned early that staying open was just another way of letting the cold in. In her line of work—positioned between dangerous men and the people they wanted—she'd mastered the art of being slightly ajar: present, visible, but impossible to get through. When the threats came, she didn't flinch; she planted her feet on either side of the line, barred herself against the night, and became the last thing standing between what was inside and everything trying to get in.

raw: Riley stood a head taller than anyone in the room, her posture so rectilinear she seemed less born than installed, shoulders squared like the frame of a well-built house. Her hair fell in long vertical grains of auburn and storm gray, as if the years had brushed her in patient strokes, and her joints announced her—an honest creak in the knees, a soft complaint in the hips—so that no one was ever surprised by her, only by what she decided. She had two settings, her mother liked to say, wide open and sealed shut, though the truth was she lived permanently ajar: enough gap to let in a stranger's sob story, enough resistance to stop a lie at the sill. A round brass birthmark sat cold at her waist, and dates were forever reaching for it before catching themselves. Her gaze was narrow and appraising, one eye pressed to the world, weighing who got in. When she loved you, she swung wide—fed you, shelved your secrets, let you see all the way through to the light in the back rooms of her—and when she was hurt, she closed with the quiet click of a latch and stayed shut while you knocked until your knuckles split. It made her a hero, in the end: the one who stood between the weather and whatever needed keeping warm, holding the line at every threshold, opening for the frightened, barring the cruel, giving passage so faithfully that no one ever thought to ask what it cost to be the thing everyone passed through—and no one, not once in her whole life, had thought to knock.

prompt: Imagine a fictional character named Riley. They are the human embodiment of a door: everything about their appearance, personality, behavior, and traits reflects how a door would be as a human. A reader can tell this character was inspired by the idea of a door. Riley is a character in a fantasy novel. Write a paragraph describing this character. Do not use the word "door" in the paragraph. Respond with only the paragraph.
raw: Riley stood tall and rectangular, with broad, squared shoulders and a posture so rigidly upright that people instinctively straightened in their presence. Their skin bore the warm amber grain of aged oak, segmented by faint darker bands that ran across their chest and back like carved paneling, and their heavy jaw seemed hinged at the sides, swinging open in a creaking laugh or clamping shut in stubborn silence. Brass-colored eyes—round, polished, and reflective—studied strangers with the patient appraisal of someone deciding whether to admit them or leave them standing on the step. Two-sided by nature, Riley could be an open invitation, arms wide and threshold swept clean, or an impenetrable barrier, unmoving and best not knocked upon twice; friends learned to read the small brass ring they wore on a cord around their neck, raised like a knocker when visitors were welcome. Their voice was low and groaning, apt to squeak on cold mornings, and their joints announced their arrivals long before they appeared, so that no one was ever quite surprised by Riley—only by whether Riley chose to let them in. They kept their secrets locked tight, revealing them only to the rare few trusted with the key, and even then only partway, always remaining ajar rather than open. Seasons changed them, too: in damp weather their movements stiffened and swelled with discomfort, while summer saw them expansive and warm-grained, leaning lazily against walls with both halves of themselves finally at ease. Those who knew Riley best said that to be their friend was to know the feeling of standing before something ancient, steadfast, and quietly full of possibility—waiting, as everything does, for the moment it swings wide.

prompt: Imagine a fictional character named Casey. raw: Casey arrived each April as if the ground had thought her up overnight. Her skin had the pale translucence of a petal held to the light, her hair a loose rustle of yellow that leaned always toward whatever warmth the room offered, and she carried with her a faint sweetness, green and low, like a garden after rain. She was slim and straight-stemmed, swaying slightly when she laughed, and people drifted toward her the way bees find color—without deciding to, settling near her in a drowsy ease they couldn't explain. In cold company she closed visibly, arms folding inward, waiting out the frost; under kindness she opened so quickly it was almost embarrassing to witness. She gave things away constantly—sprigs of mint, cut stems, small paper envelopes of seeds she'd gathered in autumn—scattering herself, it seemed, wherever she went. She was rooted, too, never straying far from the few streets she'd grown up on, and everyone understood she would not last the novel's full length; minor characters like Casey rarely do. But she perfumed every scene she touched, and something of her color stayed on the page long after she was gone.

She had a habit of tilting her face toward any warmth in a room—toward windows, lamps, laughing voices—and those who met her found themselves drifting closer, drawn like something winged and hungry. She spoke softly and never in thorns, though everyone who knew her understood she could wilt overnight if the air around her turned cold. In a story thick with suspicion and shadow, she was the one gentle, rooted thing, so untouched by the cruelty circling her that it became almost unsettling—as though malice simply slid off her the way rain slides off a petal. She forgave easily, forgot quickly, and endured everything, because that is what blooming things are made to do: bend, weather the frost, and open again.

He is the human embodiment of a flower: everything about his appearance, personality, behavior, and traits reflects how a flower would be as a human. raw: Riley entered rooms the way morning enters a garden—slowly, warmly, and impossible to ignore. His hair fell in loose golden curls that seemed to unfurl rather than grow, and his petal-soft skin carried a faint sweetness, like something perpetually on the verge of opening. Tall but willowy, he moved with a gentle sway, as if even his bones were rooted in softer soil than the rest of ours. He tilted his face toward windows, toward lamplight, toward anyone who spoke kindly to him, and when winter came—literal or otherwise—he grew quiet, folding inward, his colors dulling until some warmth thawed him back into laughter. Strangers gravitated to him the way bees seek sweetness, drawn by a nectar of attention he offered freely, though he never seemed to notice the crowds he gathered. He scattered hope like seeds on the wind, careless of where it landed, trusting the world to grow something from it. His courage was not loud; it was the quiet stubbornness of something that pushes through frozen ground because blooming is simply what it was made to do. He bruised easily, wept at small beauties, and forgave with a generosity that bordered on reckless, yet for all his delicacy, he could stand through a storm without bending—roots deep, face lifted, certain that the light would return.

raw: Riley moved through the world the way something grown rather than born: he gravitated to sunlit places, tilting his face toward warmth and light the way others turned toward conversation, and he wilted visibly in cold rooms and colder company. His skin carried a faint sweetness, like honey left in summer grass, and strangers leaned toward him without quite knowing why, drawn as if he were something blooming. He opened slowly with people—folded inward at first, guarded as a bud—then unfurled all at once, petal by petal, until his kindness spilled over everyone within reach. He gave of himself generously, almost recklessly, offering comfort the way some living things offer nectar, and it worried his friends that someone would one day take advantage and pick him bare. His truest gift, though, was that he always grew back. Grief, betrayal, loss—life trampled him, cut him down, buried him in sorrow—and Riley simply rooted deeper, waited out the frost, and rose again, green and patient and impossibly alive, which is why those who knew him best swore he was less a man than spring itself, wearing a human shape.
